question: A 3-year-old child referred for genetic consultation to assess psychomotor retardation, language delay and hyperactivity without significant dysmorphic features or associated malformations. He is the first child of a healthy, young and non-consanguineous couple. A maternal uncle has mental retardation and the maternal grandmother presented early ovarian failure. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be the most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?

options.opa: Genetic study of triplet expansion of the FMR1 gene.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Child presents with psychomotor retardation" -> "Possible genetic etiology" -> "Family history of mental retardation" -> "Maternal uncle has mental retardation" -> "Suggests possible hereditary condition" -> "FMR1 gene associated with Fragile X syndrome" -> "Genetic study of triplet expansion of the FMR1 gene is appropriate" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Child exhibits language delay and hyperactivity" -> "Developmental disorders may have genetic basis" -> "Family history includes early ovarian failure" -> "Possible involvement of X-linked conditions" -> "FMR1 gene triplet expansion linked to Fragile X syndrome" -> "Genetic study of triplet expansion of the FMR1 gene is most relevant" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Child has no significant dysmorphic features" -> "Less likely to be a chromosomal abnormality" -> "High resolution karyotype may not be necessary" -> "Family history suggests genetic disorder" -> "FMR1 gene testing is indicated" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Psychometric evaluation assesses cognitive function" -> "Does not establish a genetic diagnosis" -> "Genetic testing needed for definitive diagnosis" -> "FMR1 gene triplet expansion testing is most appropriate" -> 75%
analysis: The clinical presentation of psychomotor retardation, language delay, and hyperactivity, along with a family history of mental retardation in a maternal uncle and early ovarian failure in the maternal grandmother, suggests a possible genetic condition. The FMR1 gene is associated with Fragile X syndrome, which is a common cause of intellectual disability and can also be linked to hyperactivity. Given the family history and symptoms, testing for triplet expansion of the FMR1 gene is the most appropriate diagnostic test to establish a diagnosis.
